description: Master source utility, compare interpretations and write the exam essay on 1920s USA.
content_html:
Understanding the Exam Paper

This unit is examined through a mix of source-based questions, interpretation questions and extended essay questions. Understanding exactly what each question type demands is as important as knowing your content. This lesson brings together the skills you have been developing across the unit — source utility, comparing interpretations, explaining causes and consequences, and arguing in extended essays — and shows you how to apply them under exam conditions.

Exam questions on this unit will draw on the full range of topics: immigration and the Red Scare, religion and race, Prohibition and organised crime, the economic boom, the Wall Street Crash, popular entertainment, women’s changing roles, Native Americans and the “nation of contrasts” debate. The skills tested change by question type, so you need to know which skill each question is testing — and resist the temptation to write everything you know.

Key Fact

A top-band source utility answer must combine three elements: content (what the source actually says or shows), provenance (who produced it, when, why and for what audience) and contextual knowledge (what you know from your own study that confirms or challenges the source). Mentioning only provenance — “it is biased because Capone had a reason to lie” — is the most common error and will cap you at the lower mark bands.

Applying Source Utility: The Five-Step Method

When answering a source utility question, follow these five steps. First, identify the specific enquiry the question asks about — “useful for finding out about…” requires a specific focus. Second, examine what the source content tells you directly. Third, analyse the provenance: who made it, when, why and for whom. Fourth, use your contextual knowledge to confirm or challenge the source — does what you know from your study support or limit what the source shows? Fifth, make an overall judgement about the extent of the source’s usefulness.

Consider a typical source for this unit: a Ku Klux Klan recruitment poster from the mid-1920s. The content tells you what the Klan said it stood for — “100% American,” Protestantism, anti-immigration. The provenance tells you it was created by the Klan to recruit members — so it presents the most attractive version of the Klan’s message and omits its violence and corruption. Your contextual knowledge tells you that: the Klan reached 4–5 million members by the mid-1920s (confirming that the appeal was real); that it used terror, murder and arson (challenging any impression that it was simply a patriotic organisation); and that its appeal drew on nativist fears of immigration, urbanisation and racial mixing.

Consider a cartoon published in a temperance organisation’s newspaper in 1921, showing a father spending his wages on drink while his children starve. This source might be useful for an enquiry into why Prohibition was introduced — its content shows the temperance argument that alcohol destroys family life; its provenance (temperance publication) means it presents the anti-alcohol case in its strongest form and will omit evidence of the harms caused by Prohibition itself; your contextual knowledge tells you that the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League did genuinely argue for Prohibition on exactly these grounds, supporting the source’s usefulness for understanding the case for the ban.

The same source would be much less useful for an enquiry into whether Prohibition succeeded, because: (a) it was produced by Prohibition supporters before the problems were known; (b) its purpose was propaganda, not neutral reporting; and (c) your contextual knowledge shows that Prohibition spectacularly failed to stop drinking, creating speakeasies and organised crime instead. A strong utility answer always specifies the enquiry and adjusts the assessment accordingly.

Key Fact

On a “Compare Interpretations” question, the top mark band requires you to explain why interpretations differ. The three main reasons are: time of writing (when was the historian writing, and what did they know?); sources used (what evidence did they draw on?); and purpose and standpoint (who was the historian, and why were they writing this?). Simply describing what each interpretation says is the mid-band response.

Writing the Extended Essay: Structure and Technique

Extended essay questions — whether 12-mark “How far do you agree” or 16-mark “How far… / Account for…” — reward clear structure, specific evidence and a substantiated overall judgement. The most common mistake is describing two sides without reaching a conclusion. Examiners specifically look for a judgment that goes beyond “both sides have merit” — you need to say which side is more convincing, and why, backed by evidence.

Use the following structure for extended essays. First, a brief introduction that signals your overall argument — do you agree, partly agree or disagree? Second, paragraphs that develop points in favour of the statement, each with specific evidence. Third, paragraphs that develop points against the statement or in favour of an alternative argument, each with specific evidence. Fourth, a conclusion that reaches and justifies your overall judgement. The StudyVault rubric for extended essays describes top-band responses (Mastering) as having “a sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis.”

The strongest extended essay answers draw on multiple topics from the unit rather than treating each lesson as a separate silo. For a question about whether the United States truly was a “nation of contrasts,” the top-band answer would connect: immigration restriction and the Red Scare (fear and prejudice); the KKK and Jim Crow (racial violence); farm poverty alongside Wall Street boom (economic inequality); Native American reservation poverty alongside consumer culture; Sacco and Vanzetti’s execution alongside democratic ideals; flappers’ limited freedom alongside the continued exclusion of Black and working-class women.

Synthesis means showing that these topics are not isolated incidents but together form a pattern that either supports or challenges the overall historical argument. Examiners reward students who can hold the whole unit in their head and deploy evidence selectively to build an argument, rather than students who write everything they know about one topic.
exam_tip_html: The three questions students most often lose marks on in this unit: (1) Source utility — always use content AND provenance AND your own contextual knowledge; provenance alone is not enough. (2) Compare Interpretations — explain WHY the interpretations differ (author, time, sources, purpose) not just what they say. (3) Extended essay — always reach a specific, evidenced conclusion; “it is hard to say” is not a top-band ending. For the 12 or 16-mark essays, writing in the first person or as a personal diary entry will cap your explanation and analysis marks — write as a structured analytical essay with an argument, evidence and conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Source utility answers must combine content, provenance AND contextual knowledge. Top-band answers make a specific judgement about the source’s usefulness for the named enquiry — not a general statement about bias.
  • Compare Interpretations answers must explain WHY interpretations differ: time of writing, sources used, and the author’s purpose and standpoint. Describing how they differ (what they say) is a mid-band response.
  • Extended essays require a clear structure (argument, evidence for, evidence against, substantiated conclusion) and synthesis across the whole unit. Selecting evidence from multiple topics to build a coherent argument is the mark of a top-band response.

practice_questions.text: A source shows a photograph of a queue of unemployed men outside a soup kitchen in New York in November 1929. What can you learn from this source about the consequences of the Wall Street Crash?
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying what the source shows; one mark for development.
Example: The source shows that the Wall Street Crash had caused mass unemployment within weeks [1], with people who had previously had jobs now relying on charity for food — evidence of the rapid and severe human impact on ordinary Americans. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A source is a cartoon published in a Prohibition campaigners' newspaper in 1925, showing a criminal selling alcohol from a speakeasy while a police officer looks the other way.
How useful is this source for understanding the failure of Prohibition?
Explain your answer, using the source and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and contextual knowledge; makes a specific judgement about usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Uses at least two of the three elements with some judgement.
Developing: Mainly describes the source; limited use of provenance or context.
Emerging: Simple points about what the source shows.
Content: shows corruption of law enforcement and operation of speakeasies — useful evidence of failure.
Provenance: produced by Prohibition campaigners — likely to emphasise failures to demand stricter enforcement, so may exaggerate corruption; does not represent the pro-alcohol perspective.
Context: by 1925, approximately 30,000 speakeasies in New York City alone; Prohibition agents only 1,500 nationwide; Al Capone's Chicago Outfit earning $60 million annually — source's content is consistent with this knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of the Ku Klux Klan in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail and a developed link.
Developing: Names a cause without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid causes: fear of immigration and cultural change among white Protestants; 1915 film 'Birth of a Nation' romanticising the Klan; nativist hostility to Catholics, Jews and immigrants; economic competition from Black workers migrating north; weak federal enforcement of civil rights laws; revival by William Joseph Simmons at Stone Mountain, Georgia.

practice_questions.text:
Look at the two interpretations of the 1920s United States below.
Interpretation 1: 'The 1920s was a decade of social liberation, economic dynamism and popular culture that transformed American life.' (Frederick Lewis Allen, 1931)
Interpretation 2: 'The 1920s was characterised as much by cultural anxiety, racial violence and economic inequality as by the prosperity that is usually remembered.' (Lynn Dumenil, 1995)
Why do these two historians offer different interpretations of the 1920s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses primarily on WHY they differ — time of writing, sources, purpose and standpoint — with specific evidence from both interpretations and contextual knowledge.
Secure: Explains reasons for difference with relevant detail; may occasionally describe what they say.
Developing: Describes what each says with limited explanation of the differences.
Emerging: Simple points.
Reasons: Allen wrote in 1931 as a contemporary urban journalist using personal memory — he naturally emphasised vitality; Dumenil wrote in 1995 with 60+ years of additional social and racial history scholarship, after the civil rights movement had made inequality central to historical consciousness. Sources: Allen used journalism and personal experience; Dumenil used academic social history. Purpose: Allen wrote popular history; Dumenil wrote academic analysis. Contextual knowledge: KKK 4-5 million members, Sacco-Vanzetti, Native American poverty, farm depression — all evidence Dumenil could draw on that Allen underweighted.

practice_questions.text:
'The Wall Street Crash of 1929 was the most important cause of the end of the economic boom in the United States.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: Black Thursday 24 October 1929 triggered panic selling; Black Tuesday 29 October; market fell ~40% by mid-November; bank failures followed; 25% unemployment by 1933; psychological shock ended consumer confidence overnight.
Disagreement: structural weaknesses preceded the Crash — overproduction, farm poverty throughout the decade, unequal wealth distribution, buying on margin, weak banking regulation; the Florida land bubble (1926) was an earlier warning; these were the deeper cause — the Crash was the trigger not the root cause.
Judgement: Crash was the decisive trigger but the boom had been fragile for structural reasons throughout the decade — without those weaknesses, the Crash's damage would have been limited.

practice_questions.text:
'The United States in the 1920s was a nation of contrasts, not a nation of prosperity.'
How far do you agree? In your answer you should refer to a range of evidence from across the period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument drawing on multiple topics across the unit; agrees and disagrees with specific evidence; substantiated overall judgement; clear structure.
Secure: Several relevant points with supporting evidence; judgement present; may not sustain argument consistently.
Developing: Some relevant points; limited range of evidence; judgement underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.
Agreement (contrasts): KKK 4-5 million members alongside jazz and Hollywood; Sacco-Vanzetti execution; Native American reservation poverty; farm depression throughout decade; top 5% receiving one-third of income; Black Americans excluded from prosperity; immigration restriction driven by racism.
Disagreement (genuine prosperity): real GDP growth; 40% of world manufacturing output; car ownership spread down social scale; electrification reached 70% of homes; genuine wage growth for many industrial workers; Nineteenth Amendment; Harlem Renaissance.
Judgement: 'nation of contrasts' is the more accurate description — the prosperity was real but structurally unequal and ultimately fragile; the decade ended with catastrophe precisely because the foundations of the boom were so narrow.

knowledge_checks.q: What are the three elements that a top-band source utility answer must combine?
What is the most common error students make on the 10-mark 'Compare Interpretations' question?
options: Writing too much about one interpretation
Explaining how interpretations differ instead of why they differ

knowledge_checks.q: The origin of a source — who created it, when, for what purpose and for what audience — is called its _____.
The StudyVault rubric describes the top-band extended essay response as 'Mastering': a sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and _____ analysis.
Match each question type to what it primarily tests:
right: Agree and disagree using your own contextual knowledge; reach a substantiated judgement
Content, provenance and contextual knowledge combined to judge usefulness for an enquiry
Explain WHY historians differ — time, sources, purpose and standpoint

flashcard_questions.q: What three elements must a top-band source utility answer combine?
flashcard_questions.a: Content (what the source says), provenance (who made it, when, why) and contextual knowledge.
The origin of a source — who created it, when, for what purpose and for what audience.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the most common error on the 'Compare Interpretations' question?
flashcard_questions.a: Explaining how interpretations differ (what they say) instead of why they differ.

flashcard_questions.q: What three factors explain why historical interpretations differ?
flashcard_questions.a: Time of writing, sources used, and the author's purpose and standpoint.

flashcard_questions.q: What must an extended essay conclusion do to reach the top mark band?
flashcard_questions.a: Reach a specific, evidenced judgement — not just say 'both sides have merit'.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'synthesis' mean in the context of extended essay writing?
flashcard_questions.a: Drawing evidence from multiple topics across the unit to build a coherent argument, not treating each topic in isolation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the StudyVault Mastering standard for extended essay responses?
flashcard_questions.a: A sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a source utility answer specify the enquiry being asked about?
flashcard_questions.a: The same source can be highly useful for one enquiry and much less useful for another — the assessment must match the question.

flashcard_questions.q: What structure should an extended essay follow?
flashcard_questions.a: Brief introduction stating your argument; evidence for; evidence against; substantiated conclusion.

flashcard_questions.q: What writing style should you avoid in extended essay responses?
flashcard_questions.a: First person or diary-entry style — write as a structured analytical essay with argument, evidence and conclusion.

glossary_terms.definition: A question type asking how useful a source is as evidence for a specific enquiry, requiring analysis of content, provenance and contextual knowledge.
The origin of a source — who created it, when, for what purpose and for what audience — which affects how the source should be evaluated.
The StudyVault mark scheme tiers, from highest to lowest: Mastering, Secure, Developing and Emerging — each describing the quality of argument, evidence and judgement in an extended response.
The factual knowledge from your own study that you apply to a source or interpretation question to confirm, challenge or extend what the source shows.
In essay writing, the skill of drawing evidence from multiple topics across the unit to build a coherent argument, rather than treating each topic in isolation.
A structured written response that builds an argument, supports it with specific evidence and reaches a substantiated conclusion — the expected format for extended essay questions.

items.title: Crash Course US History — Synthesis and Review
items.description: Crash Course US History episodes on the 1920s provide excellent content to draw on when practising synthesis across the unit's key themes of boom, bust and inequality.

items.title: The Great Gatsby (1974)
items.description: Watching an interpretation of the 1920s on screen — and asking who it focuses on, what it omits and why — is a practical exercise in the source utility skills this lesson develops.

items.title: Killers of the Flower Moon (2023)
items.description: Scorsese's film about the Osage murders of the 1920s is itself an interpretation of the period — consider how it challenges the 'Roaring Twenties' narrative and why it was made when it was.

items.title: Britannica — Historiography
items.description: An essential reference for understanding why historical interpretations differ, covering the key factors: time of writing, sources, purpose and the author's standpoint.

items.title: Britannica — History (Discipline Overview)
items.description: An overview of history as a discipline, useful background for understanding what historians do, how they use evidence and why their interpretations vary.

items.title: Britannica — Volstead Act
items.description: The law that implemented Prohibition — a key source topic for this unit, and a good case study for practising source utility analysis using temperance and anti-Prohibition sources.

items.title: Britannica — Ku Klux Klan
items.description: Detailed background on the KKK in the 1920s — ideal contextual knowledge to deploy when evaluating sources about nativism or when writing extended essays on the 'nation of contrasts' thesis.
